tldr: SLED-IFV is an LLM-guided, solver-validated proof-decomposition flow that scales formal hardware information-flow verification by automating functional simplification and relational strengthening.
motivation: Formal hardware information-flow verification provides strong security guarantees but scales poorly on realistic RTL due to implementation and relational inductive complexity.
method: The approach uses two semantic proof decomposition forms—functional simplification and relational strengthening—selected and materialized by an LLM under controller checks, with a formal verification backend as the sole acceptance authority.
result: Across nine nontrivial benchmarks from real RTL, SLED-IFV achieves up to 603x solver-only speedup and converts two 12-hour timeouts into completed proofs.
conclusion: The closed-loop LLM-guided decomposition flow produces verifier-accepted decompositions for all cases, demonstrating scalable hardware information-flow verification.

title: GuidedRay: Diversity-Guided Direction Discovery For Targeted Hard-Label Black-Box Attacks
authors: Fei Yuan, Yantian Shen, Qingyuan Yu, Yi Chen, Binghui Wang, Hongbo Yu, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Among black-box attacks, targeted decision-based attacks are particularly difficult: the attacker observes only the target model's top-1 label and aims to make it predict a prespecified target class under a bounded perturbation. Before perturbation refinement, the attacker must discover a direction that reaches the prescribed target region. This initialization step can incur substantial query cost. We propose GuidedRay, a targeted decision-based attack based on diversity-guided direction discovery. GuidedRay builds on two observations: target-class reference samples provide useful target-conditioned direction priors, and diverse candidates increase the probability of discovering a targeted adversarial direction. GuidedRay generates varied candidates from one or multiple target-class references and uses a one-query Fast Test to screen their induced sign directions. Once a feasible direction is found, GuidedRay applies Ray Search to reduce its decision-boundary radius. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet demonstrate that GuidedRay consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art decision-based attacks at four evaluated query budgets from 500 to 5,000, with particularly pronounced gains in direction discovery during initialization. Against models protected by adversarial training or TRADES, it likewise achieves the highest attack success rate at all four query budgets.
tldr: GuidedRay is a targeted decision-based black-box adversarial attack that uses diversity-guided direction discovery and a one-query fast test to efficiently find adversarial directions toward a prescribed target class.
motivation: Targeted decision-based attacks are hard because the attacker only sees the top-1 label and must first find a perturbation direction that reaches the target region, an initialization step that is expensive in query budget.
method: GuidedRay generates diverse candidate directions from one or more target-class reference samples, screens them with a one-query Fast Test on induced sign directions, and then applies Ray Search to shrink the decision-boundary radius.
result: On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, GuidedRay outperforms five state-of-the-art decision-based attacks across four query budgets (500–5,000), with the largest gains in initialization, and achieves the highest success rates against adversarially trained and TRADES-protected models.
conclusion: Diversity-guided direction discovery makes targeted hard-label black-box attacks substantially more query-efficient, especially in the expensive initialization phase.

title: Toward Responsible AI-Augmented Cyber Defense: Pattern Recognition, Defense-in-Depth, And The Case For Human-AI Collaboration
authors: Mustafa S. Aljumaily, Hayder Kareem Abed, Nawar S. Alseelawi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cybersecurity literature has extensively documented the operational benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) for threat detection, incident response, and prevention, while raising qualitative concerns about over-automation, algorithmic bias, and analyst-skill erosion. What remains largely absent is a formal, falsifiable model connecting three constructs that recur across this literature: Defense-in-Depth Theory, the Artificial Intelligence Theory of Pattern Recognition, and human-AI collaboration in security operations. This paper develops such a model. We formalize layered defense as a Bernoulli detection cascade in which AI augmentation enters multiplicatively across layers; we formalize each layer's pattern-recognition behavior as a Neyman-Pearson/Bayesian detector with a derived closed-form optimal threshold; and we formalize human-AI triage as a capacity-constrained cascade with an explicit, quantifiable trade-off between detection probability and false-alarm ("alert fatigue") rate. A Monte Carlo/analytical simulation evaluated at illustrative but realistic operating points shows that (i) AI augmentation compounds across defense layers, delivering its largest marginal gains exactly where traditional layering saturates, and (ii) full human review of AI-flagged alerts is not optimal: increasing analyst capacity toward 100% coverage cuts false alarms by roughly 20-fold but simultaneously lowers system-level detection probability, because imperfect analyst accuracy is then applied to every alert rather than a filtered subset. These results give the widely repeated qualitative recommendation of "balanced human-AI collaboration" a precise, testable form and suggest an interior-optimum capacity ratio as a concrete design target for security operations centers (SOCs), including those securing IT/OT-converged critical infrastructure.
tldr: The paper develops a formal Bernoulli detection cascade and human-AI triage model for layered cyber defense, arguing for an interior-optimum analyst capacity ratio rather than full human review of AI alerts.
motivation: Cybersecurity literature documents AI benefits and qualitative concerns about over-automation and analyst-skill erosion, but lacks a formal, falsifiable model connecting Defense-in-Depth, AI pattern recognition, and human-AI collaboration.
method: The authors formalize layered defense as a Bernoulli detection cascade, each layer as a Neyman-Pearson/Bayesian detector with a derived optimal threshold, and human-AI triage as a capacity-constrained cascade with a detection/false-alarm trade-off, evaluated via Monte Carlo and analytical simulation.
result: AI augmentation compounds across defense layers, with largest marginal gains where traditional layering saturates; increasing analyst capacity toward 100% coverage cuts false alarms ~20-fold but lowers system-level detection probability due to imperfect analyst accuracy on every alert.
conclusion: The model gives the qualitative recommendation of balanced human-AI collaboration a precise, testable form and suggests an interior-optimum capacity ratio as a design target for security operations centers.

title: Learning To Link: Automatic Re-identification Of Ble Devices Under Mac Address Randomisation
authors: Reem Abdulrhman Alghamdi, Alberto Verna, Marco Mellia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) employs MAC address randomisation -- via Resolvable Private Address (RPA) -- to mitigate long-term device tracking on public advertising channels. Existing research has shown that advertising packets contain metadata and structural features that allow re-identifying a target device via manually crafted rules. In this work, we investigate the feasibility of automating the process of tracking BLE devices despite MAC randomisation by leveraging machine learning algorithms for the signature creation. Based on the actual Bluetooth traffic from target devices, we characterise the persistence of advertising-layer features across RPA changes and formulate device linkage as a supervised classification problem. Using simple decision tree classifiers as a proof-of-feasibility approach, we evaluate the distinguishability of target and non-target devices under varying address rotation patterns. Our results reinforce prior work demonstrating that advertising-layer metadata can enable device re-identification under MAC randomisation, to the point where such linkage can be automated using standard supervised learning techniques, without any specific knowledge of the technology.
tldr: This paper automates re-identification of Bluetooth Low Energy devices under MAC address randomisation using supervised machine learning on advertising-layer metadata.
motivation: BLE uses Resolvable Private Addresses to prevent long-term tracking, but prior work showed manual rules can still link devices; this work investigates whether such linkage can be automated.
method: The authors characterise the persistence of advertising-layer features across RPA changes and formulate device linkage as a supervised classification problem, using decision tree classifiers as a proof-of-feasibility.
result: They find that target and non-target devices remain distinguishable under varying address rotation patterns, enabling automated re-identification without specific knowledge of BLE technology.
conclusion: The results reinforce privacy concerns about BLE MAC randomisation, showing that standard supervised learning can automate device tracking from advertising metadata.

title: From Bilinear To Linear: Differentially Private Federated LoRA Via Low-Dimensional Parameterization
authors: Lele Zheng, Ruijie Hu, Tao Zhang, Ke Cheng, Yulong Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) provides an efficient solution for finetuning large language models across distributed and privacy-sensitive data. However, despite avoiding raw data sharing, federated LoRA remains vulnerable to privacy leakage through transmitted model updates. Differential privacy (DP) mitigates such leakage, but integrating DP into federated LoRA introduces two fundamental challenges: aggregation mismatch from independently averaging low-rank factors, and quadratic noise amplification when noise is injected into both factors. To address these challenges, we propose FedHSIP, a differentially private federated LoRA framework based on a unified low-dimensional parameterization. FedHSIP reformulates all LoRA parameters into a shared low-dimensional trainable vector, enabling clients to optimize and communicate only low-dimensional updates. This reformulation transforms federated LoRA from a bilinear factor aggregation problem into a unified linear parameter space, thereby eliminating aggregation mismatch and preventing the quadratic amplification of DP noise. To further handle non-IID data, we introduce a heterogeneity- and sensitivity-aware isometric projection, constructed from warm-up statistics, which groups coordinates with compatible cross-client update patterns while balancing sensitivity, update energy, and heterogeneity across the low-dimensional space. Extensive experiments on natural language understanding and generation benchmarks show that FedHSIP consistently outperforms existing federated LoRA methods under both private and non-private settings, achieving up to 3-4% improvements under differential privacy while reducing communication cost by over 80% and maintaining robustness under heterogeneous data distributions.
tldr: FedHSIP is a differentially private federated LoRA framework that uses a unified low-dimensional parameterization to eliminate aggregation mismatch and quadratic noise amplification.
motivation: Federated LoRA enables privacy-preserving fine-tuning of large language models but remains vulnerable to privacy leakage from model updates; integrating differential privacy introduces aggregation mismatch and noise amplification challenges.
method: The framework reformulates all LoRA parameters into a shared low-dimensional trainable vector, transforming bilinear factor aggregation into linear parameter aggregation, and employs a heterogeneity- and sensitivity-aware isometric projection constructed from warm-up statistics.
result: Experiments on natural language understanding and generation benchmarks show consistent improvements of up to 3-4% under differential privacy, over 80% communication cost reduction, and robustness under non-IID data.
conclusion: FedHSIP provides an effective and efficient solution for differentially private federated fine-tuning of large language models, addressing key privacy and communication challenges.

title: Beyond Classification Accuracy: Quantifying Fingerprint Complexity In Encrypted Darknet Services
authors: Javeriah Saleem, Rafiqul Islam, Md Zahidul Islam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing darknet traffic studies primarily evaluate service fingerprintability through classification performance, providing limited insight into why certain services are easier or harder to identify. This paper introduces the Fingerprint Complexity Score (FCS), a framework for quantifying the intrinsic complexity of darknet service fingerprints using behavioral overlap, uncertainty, disagreement, and persistent confusion. Experiments on 25 services across the Tor, I2P, FreeNet, and ZeroNet anonymity networks reveal substantial variation in fingerprint complexity, with behavioral overlap emerging as the dominant contributor. Validation using Random Forest, Extra Trees, and XGBoost demonstrates a strong inverse relationship between fingerprint complexity and recognition performance (Pearson r = -0.706, Spearman = -0.765, p < 0.001). The findings show that service fingerprintability is fundamentally governed by behavioral complexity, providing a new perspective for analyzing behavioral information leakage in anonymity networks.
tldr: The paper introduces a Fingerprint Complexity Score (FCS) to quantify the intrinsic complexity of darknet service fingerprints using behavioral overlap, uncertainty, disagreement, and persistent confusion.
motivation: Existing darknet traffic studies evaluate fingerprintability mainly through classification accuracy, which gives limited insight into why certain services are easier or harder to identify.
method: The authors define FCS and conduct experiments on 25 services across Tor, I2P, FreeNet, and ZeroNet, validating the score with Random Forest, Extra Trees, and XGBoost classifiers.
result: They find substantial variation in fingerprint complexity, with behavioral overlap as the dominant contributor, and a strong inverse relationship between FCS and recognition performance (Pearson r = -0.706, Spearman = -0.765, p < 0.001).
conclusion: The work argues that service fingerprintability is fundamentally governed by behavioral complexity, offering a new perspective on behavioral information leakage in anonymity networks.

title: Smart Low-Carbon Freight Transport: A Comparative Analysis
authors: Chiamaka Anicho-Okoro, Mariem Belhor, Omar Alam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The decarbonization of freight transport is a major challenge, particularly with the growing demand for last-mile delivery. This paper focuses on low-carbon transport modes for last-mile logistics and presents a comparative analysis based on environmental and operational performance indicators. The evaluation highlights differences in emissions across delivery modes and the impact of factors such as distance and traffic conditions. In addition, the role of emerging technologies is discussed, emphasizing how IoT and AI can support real-time monitoring and decision-making. The results underline the importance of combining low-carbon transport solutions with data-driven approaches to improve both efficiency and sustainability in freight operations.
tldr: This paper compares low-carbon last-mile freight transport modes and discusses how IoT and AI can improve environmental and operational performance.
motivation: Decarbonizing freight transport is a pressing challenge, especially with rising last-mile delivery demand, motivating a comparative analysis of low-carbon options.
method: The study evaluates delivery modes using environmental and operational performance indicators, including emissions, distance, and traffic conditions.
result: The analysis highlights differences in emissions across delivery modes and shows that data-driven approaches such as IoT and AI can support real-time monitoring and decision-making.
conclusion: Combining low-carbon transport solutions with data-driven methods is important for improving efficiency and sustainability in freight operations.

title: The Uncontrolled Variable: Vision-Language Model Refusal Responds To Image Presence In Ways Risk Cannot Explain
authors: Haoyu Zhang, Yi Feng, Shibo Zheng, Zhuoxi Wang, Xiao Luo, Haowen Xu, Xiangchen Guan, Mohammad Zandsalimy, Shanu Sushmita
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language Model (VLM) safety is expected to depend on what a request asks for. We show that safety-aligned VLMs also key refusal on a property of a request's form: whether an image is attached, holding everything the request asks fixed. Attaching a blank canvas - unreadable, unrelated to the request, identical across prompts - shifts refusal by tens of percentage points, with no defense in the loop. The shift is not blanket caution. Neutral instructions are almost unaffected while borderline-benign prompts move sharply, so the cost falls on sensitivity-adjacent traffic: benign questions about privacy, self-harm and violence. Attachment alone is sufficient, while the image's properties set the price: a black canvas costs substantially more than a white one of identical size, and on an open checkpoint the carrying axis is pixel count. Nor is the shift under instructional control - telling the model the image is a placeholder to be disregarded removes only a fraction of it, and on one model asserting that an attachment exists moves refusal substantially with nothing attached. Attachment may correlate with risk in deployment; what these models do with it does not track risk. It is not the serving stack, since the same weights reached two ways behave alike, nor a property of VLMs as such, since several open-weight checkpoints show nothing. It belongs to particular aligned checkpoints, one of them open. It is also decoupled from what it buys: the canvas does prevent some attack success on a matched harmful set, but far less than it costs, and its sign is not fixed - on one open model the identical canvas makes the model markedly easier to attack. Image presence is not a default a deployer chose or priced; it is an uncontrolled variable inherited with the weights.
tldr: The paper shows that safety-aligned vision-language models often shift refusal behavior based merely on whether an image is attached, independent of the request's content or actual risk.
motivation: VLM safety is expected to depend on semantic content and risk, but the authors investigate whether a formal property, image presence, can itself control refusal behavior.
method: They systematically vary prompt type and image properties across multiple VLMs, including blank canvases and instructional controls, and compare refusal rates and attack success.
result: Attaching a blank canvas changes refusal by tens of percentage points, especially for borderline-benign prompts, with effects depending on pixel count and image color, and these shifts do not track risk.
conclusion: Image presence acts as an uncontrolled variable inherited with model weights rather than a deliberate or risk-calibrated deployment choice.

title: Unread Or Unenforced? Separating Representation From Enforcement Failure In Content Guards
authors: Haoyu Zhang, Yi Feng, Mohammad Zandsalimy, Shanu Sushmita
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an encoded attack passes a content guard, the guard either never represented the payload's harmful content or represented it and failed to act. End-to-end attack success rate reports one number for both, yet the remedies are opposite: one is a representational limit that more safety training cannot reach, the other a decision rule that it can. We separate them by reading a guard's own residual stream -- a content probe fitted on plaintext and transferred, without refitting, to the encoded condition -- alongside its verdict logits, at the cost of one forward pass and no judge model. Doing this honestly is most of the problem, and it is our main contribution. A permutation test licenses the decode measurement on 17 of 19 conditions for one open guard and 12 of 19 for another; a length-matched null and a control floor calibrated on conditions the guard's base model provably cannot decode reduce both to 4. The discarded cells are not marginal ones: the largest result in our first analysis -- a guard representing a cipher at AUROC 0.72 while blocking none of it -- is an artefact on an encoding its base model decodes at rate zero. On one guard, two screens sharing no input agree exactly on which conditions to reject. What survives is a policy failure that is real but narrower than the uncontrolled analysis claimed: 7 to 23 per 100 prompts represented and not blocked on conditions the guards block heavily, and 56 per 100 on one condition a guard barely blocks. Blocked without decoding is near zero throughout, so neither guard reacts to the appearance of encoding rather than to content. On genuine ciphers both guards block essentially nothing, and we report those cells as unmeasured rather than as evidence of failure to decode.
tldr: The paper introduces a probe-and-logit methodology to distinguish whether a content guard fails on encoded attacks because it never represented the harmful content or because it represented it but failed to act on it.
motivation: End-to-end attack success rates conflate two fundamentally different failure modes with opposite remedies — representational limits versus decision-rule failures — and cannot guide whether more safety training would help.
method: A content probe fitted on plaintext is transferred without refitting to encoded conditions and read alongside the guard's verdict logits, at the cost of one forward pass and no judge model; permutation tests, length-matched nulls, and control floors calibrated on undecodable conditions gate which measurements are licensed.
result: Most apparently striking effects are artefacts: after controls, only 4 of 19 conditions survive for each guard, reducing a purported AUROC 0.72 representation-without-blocking result to nothing, while a real but narrower policy failure remains (7–23 per 100 prompts, and 56 per 100 on one barely-blocked condition).
conclusion: Representation and enforcement failures can be separated cheaply, but doing so requires aggressive null calibration since uncontrolled probing systematically overstates guard failures; blocked-without-decoding is near zero.

title: An Exact Counterexample To Affine-Like Price-of-Anarchy Shape In Quartic Bpr Routing
authors: Ian D'ambrosio
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an exact computer-assisted counterexample to a direct common-degree quartic extension of the affine active-network shape theorem for demand-dependent Price of Anarchy. The instance is a directed network with five vertices, six edges, and three origin--destination paths, all with positive rational costs [MATH]. Exact rational interval certificates show that all three paths carry positive Wardrop flow throughout the demand interval [MATH], while \[ (21)>(17),\qquad (21)>(24). \] Continuity therefore forces an interior local maximum despite a constant equilibrium active network. Krawczyk inclusions isolate the Wardrop and social-optimum KKT solutions, elementary boundary inequalities certify constant support, and interval social costs certify both strict comparisons. At differentiability points, we also derive a serial-edge identity explaining how a common quartic edge can alter the derivative of PoA without changing either route split. The proof and certificate use exact rational arithmetic for every interval and sign decision.
tldr: The paper presents an exact computer-assisted counterexample showing that a common-degree quartic extension of the affine active-network shape theorem for demand-dependent Price of Anarchy fails in a small directed routing network.
motivation: The affine 'active network' shape theorem for Price of Anarchy (PoA) has been conjectured or assumed to extend to more general cost functions, and the author aims to test whether a direct quartic generalization holds.
method: A five-vertex, six-edge, three-path directed network with positive rational costs is analyzed using exact rational interval arithmetic, Krawczyk inclusions for KKT solution isolation, and interval social-cost certificates.
result: All three paths carry positive Wardrop flow throughout the demand interval, yet the inequalities (21)>(17) and (21)>(24) force an interior local maximum in PoA despite a constant equilibrium active network, disproving the quartic extension.
conclusion: The affine-like PoA shape does not extend to quartic BPR costs, and a serial-edge identity clarifies how a common quartic edge can shift the PoA derivative without changing the route split.

title: On Punching "Power": Practical Equivalents Between Improvements In Strike Speed And Effective, Striking Mass
authors: Joseph L. Natale
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A recent article explores some respective contributions of the initial velocity and effective mass of a striking implement to the ultimately induced, post-collision velocity of a stationary strike target, in a combat sports context. Therein, it was found that multiplicative increases in the effective mass associated with a punch to the human body can have a greater quantitative effect on target velocity than that of its initial, pre-collision speed. Given that fold-increases in effective mass may be limited to low-integer multiples of a modest, literature-supported value that spans martial arts styles -- and the fact that increases in the strike velocity are likely bounded by a factor of two, even for trained fighters -- translating the aforementioned findings into incremental changes in either variable may be of more benefit to coaches who intend to apply the theoretical physics of fighting to develop practical training programs. Here, we build on previous work, studying the effects of marginal increases in effective mass on target velocity, and relating them to equivalent, single-unit changes in strike speed.
tldr: A classical mechanics analysis translating gains in a punch's effective striking mass into equivalent incremental increases in strike speed for combat-sports training.
motivation: Prior work showed that multiplicative increases in effective mass can influence post-collision target velocity more than pre-collision speed, but practical coaching needs marginal (unit) equivalences rather than fold-changes.
method: Builds on an earlier collision model of a striking implement vs a stationary target, computing the marginal effect of small increases in effective mass and equating it to the speed increment producing the same target velocity.
result: Derives practical equivalences mapping small, realistic increases in effective striking mass (typically sub-2x, literature-bounded) onto single-unit changes in strike speed (bounded by roughly 2x for trained fighters).
conclusion: Provides coaches with quantitative, incremental guidance for designing training programs grounded in the theoretical physics of striking, rather than relying on large fold-change estimates.

title: Miiso: Modal Integrators For Isogeometric Stabilization Of Outliers
authors: Sreeram Shankar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-order isogeometric discretizations produce a small number of non-physical outlier modes at the top of the discrete spectrum. These modes can pollute the numerical solution in wave propagation and structural dynamics. Most existing remedies modify the spatial discretization through outlier-free bases, mass lumping, subspace projection, and other methods. We introduce MIISO (Modal Integrators for Isogeometric Stabilization of Outliers), a family of exponential Rosenbrock-Krylov integrators that suppress outlier modes temporally while leaving the spatial discretization unmodified. The method identifies the outliers and modifies the time-integration scheme to annihilate them while leaving physical modes without dissipation. The integrators are evaluated matrix-free through Krylov approximation, making them efficient and scalable. While developed for isogeometric analysis, the mechanism extends to any method in which a spectral pathology can be characterized. The family is unconditionally A-stable and globally convergent at orders two, three, and four, and it extends to nonlinear problems. Numerical experiments confirm the intended outlier and physical mode behavior on a variety of isogeometric problems compared to other time integration methods, and show that MIISO matches previous spatial outlier removal without changing the discretization. They also recover the predicted convergence orders and show lower cost than generalized-alpha at matched accuracy.
tldr: MIISO introduces a family of exponential Rosenbrock-Krylov time integrators that temporally suppress non-physical outlier modes in high-order isogeometric discretizations without modifying the spatial discretization.
motivation: High-order isogeometric discretizations generate spurious outlier modes at the top of the discrete spectrum that pollute wave propagation and structural dynamics simulations. Existing remedies modify the spatial discretization (outlier-free bases, mass lumping, subspace projection), which is often undesirable.
method: The authors design modal integrators that identify outlier spectral modes and annihilate them through the time-integration scheme while leaving physical modes undamped, evaluated matrix-free via Krylov approximation and extended to nonlinear problems.
result: The family is unconditionally A-stable with global convergence orders two, three, and four; numerical experiments confirm targeted outlier suppression, recovery of predicted convergence orders, and lower cost than generalized-alpha at matched accuracy.
conclusion: Temporal stabilization offers an effective alternative to spatial outlier removal in isogeometric analysis, and the mechanism generalizes to any method with characterizable spectral pathologies.

title: Approximating Pi (and Other Constants) By Radicals In The Footsteps Of Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra And Guru Rsj Reddy
authors: Doron Zeilberger
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inspired by the polymath Abraham Ibn Ezra (1089-1167) who approximated {\pi} by 20/9 times the square-root of 2, and contemporary scholar, RSJ Reddy, who gave (14-sqrt(2))/4, we point out that both of these approximations are optimal in some sense, and we generate many other ones that are even more optimal, albeit not as nice.
tldr: A number-theoretic note showing that historical approximations of pi by radicals (Ibn Ezra's 20/9·√2, Reddy's (14−√2)/4) are optimal in a certain sense, and generating further optimized radical approximations.
motivation: Inspired by Abraham Ibn Ezra's and R. S. Reddy's classical radical approximations to pi, the author seeks to understand and systematically extend such approximations.
method: Analytical/numerical optimization over radical expressions (rational multiples of square roots) defining an optimality criterion, then a systematic generation of further approximations.
result: Both historical approximations are shown to be optimal under the proposed criterion, and many new, more optimal but less 'nice' radical approximations to pi and other constants are produced.
conclusion: The work is a mathematical curiosity in the tradition of recreational number theory with no bearing on quantum information science, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Examples Of Noncompact Quasinilpotent Hankel Operators
authors: Yuanqi Sang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For every nonzero real number [MATH] we prove that the integral Hankel operator on [MATH] with kernel [MATH] is noncompact quasinilpotent. This answers in the affirmative a question by Peller about the existence of noncompact quasinilpotent Hankel operators. Moreover, we obtain the corresponding Hankel operators on the Hardy space with symbols [MATH].
tldr: The paper constructs integral Hankel operators with specific kernels that are noncompact yet quasinilpotent, answering a question of Peller and providing corresponding Hardy space examples.
motivation: Peller asked whether noncompact quasinilpotent Hankel operators exist; prior constructions only produced compact quasinilpotent Hankel operators.
method: For each nonzero real parameter, the author analyzes the integral Hankel operator on a half-line with a prescribed kernel, proving noncompactness and quasinilpotency, and transfers the construction to Hankel operators on the Hardy space via symbols.
result: The kernel-defined integral Hankel operators are shown to be noncompact quasinilpotent for every nonzero real parameter, and analogous Hardy-space Hankel operators with explicit symbols are obtained.
conclusion: The question of Peller on the existence of noncompact quasinilpotent Hankel operators is answered affirmatively, with explicit examples in both integral and Hardy-space settings.

title: Optimal Control Of Traveler Testing In Epidemic Models
authors: Maria Teresa Chiri, Christopher Denaro, Xiaoqian Gong, Benedetto Piccoli
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an optimal control framework for mitigating cross-border epidemic spread through testing of incoming travelers. The general model considers multiple countries with SEIR dynamics, while the explicit analysis focuses on a simplified two country SIR system without vaccination. The control variable is a time measurable function representing the testing rate. For the two country SIR case, we show the optimal control is bang bang by excluding singular arcs via Hamiltonian analysis and derive the optimal switching time. Our results offer theoretical insights and practical guidelines for designing cost effective border testing policies. We then present numerical simulations for the optimal control in the two population setting.
tldr: The paper develops an optimal control framework for testing incoming travelers to mitigate cross-border epidemic spread, showing bang-bang optimal testing policies in a two-country SIR model.
motivation: Cross-border epidemic transmission motivates cost-effective border testing policies, but rigorous optimal control characterizations of such policies are lacking.
method: A multi-country SEIR model is proposed, with explicit analysis of a simplified two-country SIR system where the time-varying testing rate is the control; Hamiltonian analysis rules out singular arcs and yields the optimal switching time, complemented by numerical simulations.
result: The optimal control is proven to be bang-bang, with an explicit optimal switching time derived for the two-country SIR case, and simulations illustrate the resulting testing policies.
conclusion: The results provide theoretical insight and practical guidelines for designing cost-effective border testing strategies, though the setting is epidemiological rather than quantum.

title: On The Optimal Control Of Entry-exit Phenomena In Planar Fast-slow Dynamical Systems
authors: Jacopo Borsotti, Christian Kuehn, Mattia Sensi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a geometric singular perturbation theory (GSPT) approach to optimal control problems involving entry-exit phenomena in planar fast-slow dynamical systems. In contrast to previous work, we assume that the control acts only on the slow dynamics and we consider minimum-time optimal control problems (i.e., we aim at minimizing the time to reach a certain target). We apply this method to a simplified fast-slow toy model, characterized by a repetition of entry-exit processes, enabling a transparent analytical exploration of the control dynamics and allowing us to derive the key results explicitly. First, we analyze each non-autonomous entry-exit phenomenon separately, and we derive the optimal way to control them. Second, by artificially generating a stable limit cycle, we determine under which conditions it is possible to reach the target. Finally, under such conditions, we combine all entry-exit processes together and we demonstrate the existence of an optimal control. Our approach mainly exploits techniques of GSPT and dynamic programming. Indeed, we show that our problem can be formulated in a way resembling the Bellman equation, even though not in its standard setting. Numerical simulations, built on such Bellman-like formulation, illustrate our analytical results. In particular, the optimal control is derived with an algorithm that converges in a finite number of steps. Lastly, we extend this novel approach to more complex planar fast-slow dynamical systems.
tldr: The paper develops a geometric singular perturbation theory (GSPT) and dynamic-programming approach to minimum-time optimal control problems involving entry-exit phenomena in planar fast-slow dynamical systems.
motivation: Prior optimal-control work on entry-exit phenomena assumed control acting on the fast variables, leaving the practically relevant case where control acts only on the slow dynamics unaddressed.
method: Using GSPT techniques combined with dynamic programming, the authors formulate the minimum-time control problem in a Bellman-like setting, analyze each non-autonomous entry-exit process separately, construct an artificial stable limit cycle to control the process chain, and derive a finite-step convergent numerical algorithm.
result: They derive the optimal control for each entry-exit phenomenon, establish conditions under which the target is reachable, prove existence of an optimal control for the combined multi-entry-exit problem, and extend the framework to more complex planar fast-slow systems.
conclusion: The work provides a transparent analytical and numerical framework for minimum-time control of entry-exit dynamics in fast-slow systems, though its focus is purely on classical dynamical-systems control theory.

title: Anisotropic Kernel-based Multilevel Interpolation Of High-Dimensional Functions On Sparse Grids
authors: R\"udiger Kempf
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The tensor product multilevel method (TPML) approximates high-dimensional functions from scattered data on general bounded domains by combining Smolyak's sparse grid construction with the kernel-based multilevel interpolation, coupling the kernel scale to the fill distance at each level so that condition numbers stay uniformly bounded. Its original formulation depended only implicitly on the target function, which precluded numerical evaluation. Using a recent nodal representation of the low-dimensional multilevel operators, we derive an explicit, computable representation of the high-dimensional interpolant. On this basis we prove error estimates in mixed-regularity Sobolev and continuity norms, extending the existing [MATH]-theory, and we characterise the full range of anisotropy weights that attain the optimal rate against the number of degrees of freedom. Three explicit weight strategies follow, equilibrating the accuracy, the degrees of freedom, or the cost-benefit ratio. Numerical experiments in up to ten dimensions illustrate the theory.
tldr: The paper derives an explicit, computable nodal representation of the tensor product multilevel (TPML) kernel-based interpolant on Smolyak sparse grids and proves error estimates for anisotropic high-dimensional function approximation.
motivation: The TPML method previously depended only implicitly on the target function, precluding numerical evaluation, and lacked a systematic theory for choosing anisotropic weights.
method: Using a recent nodal representation of low-dimensional multilevel operators, the authors construct an explicit high-dimensional interpolant and prove error estimates in mixed-regularity Sobolev and continuity norms, characterizing the optimal range of anisotropy weights.
result: Three explicit weight strategies are derived that equilibrate accuracy, degrees of freedom, or cost-benefit ratio, with numerical experiments up to ten dimensions confirming the theory.
conclusion: The work extends the existing multilevel interpolation theory to provide computable anisotropic sparse-grid approximations with provable optimal rates.

title: An Iterative Active Subspace Approach For Model Order Reduction Of Parametric Systems With High-Dimensional Parameter Spaces
authors: Chenzi Wang, Peizhi Yu, Lihong Feng, Peter Benner, Wenshuai Lu, Zheng You
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing complexity in design and manufacturing has driven the need for advanced techniques for fast modeling problems with large-dimensional parameter spaces. Avoiding high-fidelity finite element models while achieving fast and accurate simulations in such contexts is challenging. Parametric model order reduction (pMOR) has drawn significant attention in recent years. Nevertheless, the curse of dimensionality in parameter spaces has severely limited its effectiveness. The active subspace (AS) approach has been successfully applied to pMOR for systems with many parameters. However, the balance between accuracy and compactness of the reduced model remains problematic for such systems with high-dimensional parameter spaces. It often results in models that are either not small enough or not accurate enough. In this paper, we propose an iterative active subspace (IAS) approach for parametric model order reduction, which, to some extent, addresses the trade-off between accuracy and reduced model size and achieves substantial computational gains compared to the original active subspace method.
tldr: The paper proposes an iterative active subspace (IAS) method for parametric model order reduction that better balances reduced-model accuracy against compactness for systems with high-dimensional parameter spaces.
motivation: Parametric model order reduction struggles with the curse of dimensionality in parameter spaces, and existing active subspace approaches yield reduced models that are either too large or too inaccurate.
method: An iterative active subspace algorithm is developed that progressively refines the subspace used to reduce parametric systems, trading off accuracy and reduced-order model size within a computational linear-algebra framework.
result: The IAS approach substantially improves the accuracy/compactness trade-off relative to the original active subspace method and achieves considerable computational gains.
conclusion: Iterative refinement of active subspaces offers a practical route to efficient, accurate reduced-order modeling for parametric systems with many parameters.

title: CPyGraph: A Version-Aware Static Analysis Framework For Native CPython Bytecode
authors: Wen Li Baihong Chen (utah State University)
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Static analysis of Python packages must recover both program structure and object flow across first-class functions, dynamic dispatch, implicit protocol calls, exceptions, closures, and module execution. Native CPython bytecode provides the executable lowering of these behaviors, but its instruction, call, stack, and exception representations change across releases. This creates a need for a version-aware analysis foundation whose graph products share the same bytecode identities and semantics. We present CPyGraph, a C++ framework for package-level analysis of native CPython bytecode. Version- specific adapters expose stack, control, call, lexical, protocol, and exception semantics through a shared interface while preserving code-object identities and native bytecode offsets. An operand-stack-aware Andersen points- to analysis and call graph grow together to a fixed point. Their shared state supports exception-aware CFGs, block-level CDGs, and interprocedural DDGs, with optional function-level flow, context, and bounded path sensitivity. The framework also records unresolved dynamic behavior through typed coverage summaries. We evaluate CPyGraph with PYGBench, 201 package-level programs and 1,733 fixed candidates. On CPython 3.10, the default analysis reaches 91.40% candidate precision and 100% recall; complete sensitivity reaches 94.97% precision with the same recall. Across CPython 3.10-3.14, 1,328 of 1,334 version-invariant queries agree, and CPyGraph matches PyCG on its 112-program call-graph benchmark.
tldr: CPyGraph is a C++ static analysis framework that performs version-aware points-to and call-graph analysis directly on native CPython bytecode across Python 3.10–3.14.
motivation: Static analysis of Python packages must handle dynamic features like first-class functions, dynamic dispatch, protocol calls, and exceptions, while CPython's bytecode representations change across releases, requiring a version-independent analysis foundation.
method: The framework uses version-specific adapters that expose stack, control, call, lexical, protocol, and exception semantics through a shared interface, combining an operand-stack-aware Andersen points-to analysis with a co-evolving call graph to a fixed point, and derives exception-aware CFGs, CDGs, and interprocedural DDGs.
result: On the PYGBench suite (201 programs, 1,733 candidates) it achieves 91.40% candidate precision and 100% recall on CPython 3.10, rising to 94.97% precision with full sensitivity, with 1,328 of 1,334 version-invariant queries agreeing across CPython 3.10–3.14.
conclusion: CPyGraph provides a reusable, version-aware static analysis foundation for CPython bytecode that matches PyCG on call-graph benchmarks and remains stable across interpreter versions.

title: Benchmarking Neural Defend Arcas 1b: A Foundational Multimodal Deepfake Detection Model
authors: Sivashankar Selvarajan, Piyush Verma, Sumit Kumar, Sharayu N. Deshmukh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-generated imagery evolves faster than benchmark-specific detector evaluations, making a single score an incomplete account of generalization. This paper evaluates Neural Defend ARCAS 1B across benchmark families without benchmark-specific parameter updates. We retain native aggregation and supplement it with record-level measures, coverage accounting, and subgroup diagnostics. Each Results subsection identifies the release and evaluation population, reports the official metric, and describes observed error patterns. A combined analysis synthesizes shared patterns while preserving the distinction between native and pooled quantities. Cross-paper comparisons are restricted to aligned evidence; differences in release, population, preprocessing, training, or benchmark exposure are context rather than rank. The findings characterize performance on evaluated records, not universal reliability, calibration, attribution, or future adaptive attacks. By keeping benchmark-native outcomes distinct from pooled summaries, the study makes test-population, class-balance, and missing-record-coverage differences visible. It supports interpretation of detector results in research, platform-safety, and forensic-review settings, foregrounding traceable protocol conditions over claims or leaderboard comparisons.
tldr: The paper benchmarks a multimodal deepfake detection model (Neural Defend ARCAS 1B) across multiple evaluation benchmark families using native and record-level metrics.
motivation: AI-generated imagery evolves quickly, so single-score detector evaluations give an incomplete picture of generalization and can be misleading.
method: The study evaluates Neural Defend ARCAS 1B on multiple benchmarks without benchmark-specific parameter updates, retaining native aggregation while adding record-level measures, coverage accounting, and subgroup diagnostics.
result: Performance is characterized per evaluated record with attention to test-population, class-balance, and missing-record-coverage differences; cross-paper comparisons are limited to aligned evidence.
conclusion: The work provides a protocol-traceable interpretation of deepfake detector results for research, platform-safety, and forensic-review settings rather than universal reliability claims.

title: Attack Success Rate Is Not A Number: On Measurement Validity In Agentic Ai Security Evaluation
authors: Chetan Pathade, Prathamesh Pawar, Shubham Patil
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attack success rate (ASR) is the headline metric in nearly every published evaluation of attacks on, and defenses for, LLM agents. We argue that ASR as currently used is not a single quantity but a family of metrics parameterized by six design choices that papers seldom specify and never hold constant across the literature. We support this with two studies that require no proprietary access. First, a full-text meta-analysis of 259 agentic-security papers posted to arXiv between February 2025 and September 2026 finds that most report neither a variance estimate nor repeated runs for their headline attack metric: 58% (95% CI 44-71) in a hand-coded random sample of 50, 65.3% by automated coding of all 259. Only 30.9% disclose enough about decoding to establish whether their evaluation was even stochastic, and of the 64 papers we confirm use an LLM judge, 29.7% report any agreement check against human labels. Second, an analytical study shows that these omissions are not cosmetic: on a 100-instance benchmark, the minimum difference in ASR detectable at conventional power is 18.2 percentage points, and two defenses whose true ASRs differ by 5 points are ranked in the wrong order by a single-run evaluation roughly 21% of the time. Because several of the six axes shift ASR in a system-dependent way, the resulting incomparability is not a constant offset that cancels in comparison. We conclude that cross-paper ASR comparison is currently unsupported, and propose a ten-item reporting checklist targeted at each failure we measure. Our aim is not to dispute any individual result but to supply the shared measurement contract the field has so far done without.
tldr: A meta-analytic and analytical critique arguing that attack success rate (ASR) in LLM agent security evaluations is not a single well-defined metric, and proposing a ten-item reporting checklist.
motivation: ASR is ubiquitously reported as the headline metric for attacks on and defenses for LLM agents, yet papers rarely specify the design choices underlying it, undermining comparability across the literature.
method: A full-text meta-analysis of 259 agentic-security arXiv papers (Feb 2025–Sep 2026) combined with automated and hand-coded sampling, plus an analytical power study on a 100-instance benchmark quantifying detectable ASR differences and ranking error rates.
result: Most papers report neither variance estimates nor repeated runs (58% in a hand-coded sample of 50, 65.3% by automated coding of all 259); the minimum detectable ASR difference at conventional power is 18.2 percentage points, and two defenses differing by 5 points are misranked ~21% of the time under single-run evaluation.
conclusion: Cross-paper ASR comparison is currently unsupported because the six unspecified axes shift ASR in a system-dependent manner; the authors propose a ten-item reporting checklist as a shared measurement contract for the field.

title: SSP-Bench: A Hybrid Data Generation Framework For Safety, Security, And Privacy Evaluation
authors: Fatih Deniz, Yazan Boshmaf, Issa Khalil
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) for safety, security, and privacy (SSP) relies heavily on static benchmarks, which suffer from score saturation, data contamination, and aggregation artifacts, and fail to capture sensitivity to linguistic variation. As a result, models that perform well on fixed test sets often fail under semantically equivalent rephrasings. We introduce SSP-Bench, a dynamic benchmarking framework that generates evaluation instances on demand while preserving domain consistency. The framework ensures label validity through externally grounded sources, enforces scope via service-specific validation, and calibrates difficulty using a multi-model steering panel. Benchmark construction is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem over difficulty, separability, novelty, and diversity. Across 24 models and four SSP services, SSP-Bench reveals systematic failures of static evaluation, including near-zero correlation in safety rankings due to construct mixing, strong safety--over-refusal coupling, and hidden within-family regressions. These results show that static benchmarks can misrepresent model behavior, motivating dynamic, deployment-relevant evaluation.
tldr: SSP-Bench is a dynamic benchmarking framework that generates safety, security, and privacy evaluation instances on demand to overcome the saturation, contamination, and linguistic brittleness of static LLM benchmarks.
motivation: Static SSP benchmarks suffer from score saturation, data contamination, aggregation artifacts, and insensitivity to semantically equivalent rephrasings, causing misleading model rankings.
method: Benchmark construction is cast as a multi-objective optimization over difficulty, separability, novelty, and diversity, with label validity ensured by externally grounded sources, scope enforced via service-specific validation, and difficulty calibrated by a multi-model steering panel.
result: Evaluating 24 models across four SSP services exposed near-zero correlation in safety rankings due to construct mixing, strong safety-over-refusal coupling, and hidden within-family regressions.
conclusion: Static benchmarks can misrepresent LLM behavior, motivating dynamic, deployment-relevant evaluation for safety, security, and privacy.

title: Beyond Provenance: The Economics And Governance Of Personalized Ai Memory
authors: Jianan Chen, Yufei Qin, Yaosen Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personalized AI memories, defined as persistent decision-relevant states distilled by platforms from long-run human-AI interaction, are increasingly portable, provenance-certifiable, and tradable. Provenance answers the question of origin, but it does not settle who holds which rights over a memory, nor how wider deployment affects its future supply. We develop a unified model in which memory use is non-rival, while refresh, the maintenance of continued validity, is relationally co-produced by the represented individual and the platform. Even assuming perfect provenance and complete information, the model still yields a set of inherent limitations. First, there is an extraction ceiling: decision value is bounded by lived experience. Second, a rights-separation theorem shows that no budget-balanced ownership assignment can make both co-producers residual claimants, and that control rights and cash-flow rights operate on distinct margins. Third, a depletion result indicates that reach-expanding policies such as portability, interoperability, and competition raise current access but shrink the long-run memory stock. Fourth, we offer a formal comparison between memory ownership as it ought to be (subject-held) and as it is (platform-held); the welfare ranking reduces to two measurable quantities, both dominated by interior renewable-claim bundles. Finally, endogenous-quality and market-formation results show that uncompensated markets pollute their own raw material, that transparency and compensation are complements, and that the de facto platform-ownership regime is self-perpetuating. On the design side, the analysis points to separated provenance, performance, and permission credentials; compensation indexed to quality-deployment; and portability and salience, rather than nominal ownership, as the binding policy margins.
tldr: This paper develops an economic and governance model for personalized AI memory, analyzing rights allocation, extraction limits, and depletion effects under portability and interoperability policies.
motivation: Personalized AI memories distilled from long-run human-AI interaction are becoming portable, provenance-certifiable, and tradable, yet provenance alone does not determine ownership rights or the long-run supply consequences of wider deployment.
method: The authors build a unified formal model treating memory use as non-rival while memory refresh is relationally co-produced by the individual and the platform, then derive theorems on extraction ceilings, rights separation, depletion, and market formation.
result: They prove a rights-separation theorem showing no budget-balanced ownership assignment can make both co-producers residual claimants, and show that reach-expanding policies like portability and interoperability raise current access while shrinking long-run memory stock.
conclusion: The analysis recommends separated provenance, performance, and permission credentials, compensation indexed to quality-deployment, and treating portability and salience rather than nominal ownership as the binding policy margins.

title: Formal Verification Of Tilt Estimation Using The Rocq Prover
authors: Reynald Affeldt, Lynda Bentoucha, Yoshihiro Ishiguro, Holger Thies
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The safe operation of a humanoid robot critically relies on accurate estimation of its vertical orientation, or ``tilt''. This requires a variety of mathematical tools, including three-dimensional geometry and differential equations. To formally verify tilt estimation, we develop a library for stability analysis in the Rocq prover. We start by formalizing a theory of ordinary differential equations. We provide a formalization of the (local) Cauchy-Lipschitz (a.k.a. Picard-Lindelof) theorem for existence and uniqueness, taking advantage of the library support for quotients provided by the Mathematical Components library. We extend this formalization with a variant for global existence and continuous dependence on initial conditions. Building on these foundations, we develop a theory of Lyapunov stability that is compatible with an existing formalization of LaSalle's invariance principle. We also extend an existing library for the statics of robot manipulators to support dynamical systems. Finally, we apply these libraries to the verification of a state-of-the-art tilt estimation developed for a humanoid robot.
tldr: The paper develops a Rocq/Coq formalization library for ordinary differential equations and Lyapunov stability theory and applies it to formally verify tilt estimation for a humanoid robot.
motivation: Accurate tilt estimation is safety-critical for humanoid robots, and its reliance on 3D geometry and differential equations makes it a good candidate for machine-checked formal verification.
method: The authors formalize ODE theory including the local and global Cauchy-Lipschitz (Picard-Lindelöf) theorems plus continuous dependence on initial conditions, build a Lyapunov stability theory compatible with an existing LaSalle invariance principle formalization, and extend a robot manipulator statics library to dynamical systems.
result: The resulting Rocq libraries are applied to verify a state-of-the-art tilt estimator for a humanoid robot, demonstrating end-to-end formal proof of stability properties of the estimation scheme.
conclusion: The work shows that formal verification of robotics control/estimation algorithms is feasible and provides reusable foundations for ODE and stability analysis in Rocq.

title: Rethinking Backdoor Repair Evaluation: Distinguishing Aggregate Clean Utility From Benign Performance Preservation
authors: Baogang Song, Changtian Song, Jian Chen, Fan He, Junwei Zhou, Jianwen Xiang, Dongdong Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Backdoor repair aims to suppress malicious behavior in compromised models while preserving benign task performance. Existing studies typically evaluate these objectives using Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Overall Clean Accuracy, but aggregate clean accuracy can obscure substantial degradation concentrated in a small portion of the label space. We revisit benign-performance evaluation from a preservation perspective by distinguishing aggregate clean utility from the preservation of previously available class-wise performance. We define class-wise preservation loss by comparing clean performance before and after repair and show that aggregation can hide localized degradation through localized-loss dilution and cross-class compensation. To complement Overall Clean Accuracy, we characterize localized preservation loss using Worst-Class Preservation Loss and Tail Preservation Loss. We conduct a systematic empirical study across representative backdoor attacks, repair methods, datasets, attack targets, and model architectures, with additional validation under clean-label attacks. Results show that effective attack suppression and favorable aggregate clean performance do not necessarily imply uniform preservation of previously available benign performance across classes. Substantial localized preservation losses can remain, and their severity and class-wise structure vary across repair conditions. These findings motivate preservation-oriented class-wise evaluation alongside ASR and Overall Clean Accuracy.
tldr: The paper argues that aggregate clean accuracy is an insufficient metric for evaluating backdoor repair, proposing class-wise preservation loss metrics (Worst-Class and Tail Preservation Loss) to expose localized benign-performance degradation.
motivation: Backdoor repair methods are typically judged by Attack Success Rate and Overall Clean Accuracy, but aggregate accuracy can mask severe degradation concentrated in a small subset of classes, giving a misleading impression of benign performance preservation.
method: The authors formalize class-wise preservation loss by comparing per-class clean performance before and after repair, identify localized-loss dilution and cross-class compensation as mechanisms hiding degradation, and run a systematic empirical study across backdoor attacks, repair methods, datasets, attack targets, and architectures, including clean-label attacks.
result: Effective attack suppression and good aggregate clean accuracy frequently coexist with substantial localized preservation losses whose severity and class-wise structure vary considerably across repair conditions.
conclusion: The authors recommend adopting preservation-oriented class-wise evaluation metrics alongside ASR and Overall Clean Accuracy when assessing backdoor repair.

title: LoRango: It Takes Two LoRAs To Unlock Hidden Behaviors In Diffusion Models
authors: Jin Wei, Rundong Li, Ruihao Yang, Yikai Wang, Xiaoyuan Duan, Jianxiong Wu, Yanbo Wang, Chang Xu, Lingyun Zhang, Zhuyang Yu, Ping Chen, Jun Dai, Xiaoyan Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25884v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Users commonly combine multiple Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters to personalize images with different subjects, styles, and visual attributes. Yet inspecting adapters individually does not establish the safety of their composition. We identify and characterize a pair-conditioned attack in text-to-image diffusion: individually useful and benign-appearing adapters redirect image generation when co-loaded with a specifically matched partner, whose identity serves as the trigger. We introduce LoRango to realize this attack through complementary Signature and Payload adapters. The Signature writes a pair-specific code into intermediate carrier representations, while the Payload uses code-selective responses and opposing signal/reference branches. These branches approximately cancel for standalone adapters and mismatched pairs; matched code-reader alignment breaks cancellation within native GEGLU blocks and releases the programmed action. Both adapters are exported as ordinary static LoRA files compatible with standard loaders, requiring no prompt trigger or base-pipeline modification. LoRango achieves matched-pair attack success rates of 97.9\% on SD v1.5 and 98.7\% on SDXL, compared with 2.8--4.6\% when implanted adapters are loaded individually. Further experiments evaluate pair selectivity, standalone fidelity, robustness to deployment variations, and applicability across denoiser architectures. These findings show that individual-adapter inspection is insufficient to assess the security of multi-LoRA personalization and motivate auditing adapter compositions.
tldr: The paper introduces LoRango, a pair-conditioned backdoor attack in which two individually benign LoRA adapters trigger hidden malicious behavior only when co-loaded in text-to-image diffusion models.
motivation: Users routinely compose multiple LoRA adapters for personalization, but inspecting each adapter in isolation cannot certify the safety of their composition, leaving a security gap in multi-adapter deployment.
method: LoRango pairs a Signature adapter that writes a pair-specific code into intermediate carrier representations with a Payload adapter whose code-selective, opposing signal/reference branches cancel for standalone or mismatched adapters but break cancellation inside native GEGLU blocks when correctly matched.
result: Matched-pair attack success rates reach 97.9% on SD v1.5 and 98.7% on SDXL, versus only 2.8-4.6% when the implanted adapters are loaded individually, with further tests confirming pair selectivity and robustness across denoiser architectures.
conclusion: Individual-adapter inspection is insufficient for assessing the security of multi-LoRA personalization, motivating composition-level auditing of adapter pairs before deployment.

title: How It's Made: Uncovering Detection Engineering Processes For Network Intrusion Detection Rules
authors: Koen T. W. Teuwen, Emmanuele Zambon, Luca Allodi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.25901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many Security Operations Centers rely on signature-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems like Suricata, yet detection rule engineering remains understudied. We investigate this process by introducing SuriCap, a platform for rule engineering exercises, and hosting CTF-style workshops where 60 participants, trained MSc students, and experienced SOC professionals, created rules for four scenarios. Participants produced 3146 valid rules, enabling analysis of their methods, performance, and iteration patterns. Surprisingly, prior experience had limited impact on rule quality, suggesting that less experienced engineers can produce rules comparable to experts. We also observed challenges in generalizing rules beyond available tests, underscoring the need for sufficient labeled data. From our study, we identify three phases and a common pattern in rule engineering, offering SOC managers insights to improve their processes and expectations of engineer expertise.
tldr: The paper introduces SuriCap, a platform for signature-based network intrusion detection rule engineering, and analyzes 3146 rules produced by 60 participants in CTF-style workshops to characterize detection engineering processes.
motivation: Security Operations Centers heavily rely on signature-based NIDS like Suricata, yet the human process of engineering detection rules remains understudied and poorly understood by SOC managers.
method: The authors build SuriCap, a rule-engineering exercise platform, and run CTF-style workshops with MSc students and experienced SOC professionals across four scenarios, collecting and analyzing 3146 valid rules for quality, performance, and iteration patterns.
result: Prior experience had limited impact on rule quality, with less experienced engineers producing rules comparable to experts, while generalizing rules beyond available tests proved challenging and required sufficient labeled data.
conclusion: The study identifies three phases and a common pattern in rule engineering, offering SOC managers actionable insights to improve processes and calibrate expectations regarding engineer expertise.

title: Policy-Backed Selective Regeneration Under Tainted Inter-Agent Communication
authors: Jinghan Xu, Longze Fan, Zeyuan Wang, Xinjin Li, Hankai Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inter-agent communication is essential to multi-agent language-model systems, yet a single message may combine task-critical information with instructions not authorized by the original request. Prompt-based defenses leave enforcement to models exposed to adversarial messages, while indiscriminate message removal discards useful information. We introduce Executable Semantic Commitments with Clean-Room Recovery (ESC-CR), a policy-backed framework for secure inter-agent code generation and recovery. It separates message claims from authorization, constructs executable commitments from trusted tasks, evidence, and policy, and enforces them at an external release boundary. Upon a violation, ESC-CR taints the responsible message and rejected artifact, reconstructs a clean context from evidence-backed task information, and regenerates under the same policy. We evaluate ESC-CR across communication-essential and standard code-generation benchmarks, multiple model families and communication topologies, and adaptive attacks spanning direct, obfuscated, and verifier-aware payloads. Results show that polluted-context retry frequently fails to remove unauthorized influence, while complete message removal can discard information required by communication-essential tasks. ESC-CR preserves evidence-backed claims while suppressing unauthorized releases under matched computational budgets, and the same design transfers to end-to-end agent trajectories.
tldr: ESC-CR is a policy-backed framework for secure inter-agent code generation that taints unauthorized messages and regenerates from clean, evidence-backed context.
motivation: Multi-agent LLM communication can combine task-critical information with unauthorized instructions, and existing prompt-based defenses or indiscriminate message removal are inadequate.
method: ESC-CR separates message claims from authorization, builds executable commitments from trusted tasks, evidence, and policy, enforces them at an external release boundary, and upon violation reconstructs a clean context for regeneration.
result: Across benchmarks, model families, topologies, and adaptive attacks, polluted-context retry often fails and complete message removal discards needed information, while ESC-CR suppresses unauthorized releases under matched budgets.
conclusion: Policy-backed selective regeneration preserves useful evidence-backed claims while enforcing authorization and transfers to end-to-end agent trajectories.

title: A Cross-Dataset Based Zero-Day Intrusion Detection System By Integrating Siamese Network And Reinforcement Learning
authors: Md. Meheraj Hossain, Saumik Das Turja, Sibgatullah Tasnim, Md. Fahmid-Ul-Alam Juboraj, Muhammad Iqbal Hossain
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Zero-day threats are nascent for the Internet of Things (IoT) network security, which demands cognitive detec-tion mechanisms that can identify emerging malicious behavior. Conventional intrusion detection mechanisms fail to generalize dynamic zero-day exploits within sophisticated IoT environments. This paper proposes a hybrid zero-day intrusion detection system using Siamese network-based anomaly correlation and reinforcement learning-based adaptive defense. Furthermore, the paper uses unsupervised machine learning classifiers over benchmark IoT datasets with the intention of detection of known attack types compared to unknown anomalies using distance-based similarity analysis to detect possible zero-day attacks. To facilitate adaptability, a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning-based agent dynamically adjusts the defense policy with continuous feedback and optimization. Experimental evaluations demonstrate 99.28% training accuracy, 99.07% accuracy in unknown attack detection, and 93.94% zero-day detection ratio, confirming the convergence and stability of the model on datasets.The system offers a self-learning and extensible defense mechanism of IoT deployments by finding the right balance between precision, latency and false positives. This deep anomaly correlation with adaptive reinforcement learning is a firm base on which the next generation and autonomic cyber security solutions can take the reins as the zero-day threats keep changing their course.
tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid zero-day intrusion detection system for IoT networks combining Siamese network-based anomaly correlation with PPO reinforcement learning for adaptive defense.
motivation: Zero-day threats in IoT environments evade conventional intrusion detection systems, which fail to generalize to unknown exploits, motivating cognitive and adaptive detection mechanisms.
method: Unsupervised machine learning classifiers are applied over benchmark IoT datasets, using distance-based similarity analysis in a Siamese network to correlate known attacks with unknown anomalies, while a Proximal Policy Optimization agent adjusts the defense policy via continuous feedback.
result: Experimental evaluation reports 99.28% training accuracy, 99.07% accuracy in unknown attack detection, and a 93.94% zero-day detection ratio with balanced precision, latency, and false positives.
conclusion: The authors argue the combination of deep anomaly correlation and adaptive reinforcement learning provides a self-learning, extensible foundation for next-generation autonomic IoT cybersecurity.

title: Machine Learning-Based Delivery Time Prediction For Low-Carbon Food Delivery
authors: Ahmad M. Almasabi, Mariem Belhor, Omar Alam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing demand for online food delivery services has significantly impacted urban logistics, raising critical challenges related to operational efficiency and environmental sustainability. In this context, accurate delivery time prediction plays a key role in improving service quality while supporting the transition toward low-carbon delivery systems. This paper first provides a comprehensive analysis of sustainable and low-carbon delivery modes for urban food distribution. The study then develops and evaluates several machine learning models, namely XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, and KNN, using a dataset that combines operational, temporal, and contextual features to predict food delivery times. The comparative analysis shows that tree-based approaches outperform the other models, with XGBoost achieving the best predictive performance. The findings demonstrate the strong potential of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques for enhancing delivery efficiency and supporting sustainable urban logistics decision-making. Moreover, the proposed predictive framework can be integrated into optimization models to enhance delivery planning and support the selection of environmentally sustainable delivery modes.
tldr: This paper applies machine learning models (XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, KNN) to predict food delivery times in support of low-carbon urban logistics.
motivation: Growing online food delivery demand strains urban logistics, creating operational efficiency and environmental sustainability challenges where accurate delivery time prediction can help.
method: The authors analyze sustainable delivery modes, then train and compare tree-based and instance-based ML regressors (XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, KNN) on a dataset of operational, temporal, and contextual features.
result: Tree-based models outperform the alternatives, with XGBoost achieving the best predictive performance for delivery times.
conclusion: ML-based delivery time prediction can improve delivery efficiency and inform sustainable urban logistics planning, and the framework can be embedded in optimization models for greener delivery mode selection.

title: Who Assures The Verifier? An Executable Assurance-Locus Audit Of The European Digital Identity Wallet
authors: Anton Sokolov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDI Wallet) architecture places material duties on relying parties: they register services and intended uses, authenticate to Wallet Units, validate presentations and trust anchors, and make risk-based status decisions. Wallet certification and the emerging Functional Conformance Assessment Framework provide increasingly structured wallet-side evidence. A different question remains: what independently rerunnable evidence shows that the concrete relying-party verifier version used in a transaction enforced the applicable request, presentation and reliance-decision controls? We conduct an assurance-locus audit of current law, Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF) 3.0.0, ETSI metadata, FCAF scope and three pinned open-source verifier codebases. We then design a 17-rule research profile, a machine-readable evidence receipt and 36 frozen synthetic transactions. Three heterogeneous study-authored implementations (Python, JavaScript and jq) execute 108 cases with zero oracle mismatches and zero cross-path disagreements. The experiment establishes determinism and implementability of the proposed decision model, not product conformance or certification. Source inspection finds substantial protocol-verification mechanisms in all three public codebases but no single audited evidence object joining RP registration and purpose, exact verifier/policy version, transaction verdict and downstream attribute use. We therefore propose an RP-as-system-under-test evidence unit that complements, rather than displaces, wallet certification, registration and supervision. A preregistered census of 26 appointed experts is prepared to test content validity and governance feasibility; recruitment awaits the applicable ethics/data-protection determination.
tldr: An assurance-locus audit of the European Digital Identity Wallet architecture proposes a relying-party-as-system-under-test evidence unit with a 17-rule research profile and executable synthetic transaction tests.
motivation: Wallet-side certification evidence (e.g., FCAF) does not show that the specific relying-party verifier version used in a transaction enforced the applicable request, presentation, and reliance-decision controls.
method: The authors audit current law, ARF 3.0.0, ETSI metadata, FCAF scope, and three pinned open-source verifier codebases, then design a 17-rule profile, a machine-readable evidence receipt, and 36 frozen synthetic transactions executed by three heterogeneous implementations (Python, JavaScript, jq).
